title: Couran Cove Resort

paragraphs.text: As the world’s population becomes increasingly urbanised, the demand for nature-based and environmentally friendly tourist attractions has grown rapidly. Couran Cove Resort is one such tourist attraction. It occupies approximately 150 hectares of South Stradbroke Island, which lies off the Gold Coast in Queensland, Australia, and is separated from the mainland by a stretch of sea three kilometres wide.

More than a century ago, there was only one Stradbroke Island, and there were at least four Aboriginal groups living there. Regrettably, most of the original island dwellers were killed by diseases at the end of the 19th century. A European ship was wrecked on the island in 1894 and was later destroyed because its cargo had included dynamite. This caused a large crater in the sandhills on Stradbroke Island. Eventually, the ocean broke through the weakened land form and it split into North and South Stradbroke Islands. Stradbroke Island was one of the world’s few naturally occurring sand islands and the two islands are now home to a wide range of plant communities and one of the largest remaining remnants of the rare Livistona rainforest left in Australia. Many mangrove and rainforest areas of South Stradbroke Island were cleared, drained or filled for residential, industrial, agricultural or urban development in the first half of the 20th century, but farmers finally abandoned South Stradbroke Island in 1939 because the nutrient-poor sandy earth made agricultural activities impossible.

Couran Cove Resort has no airstrip but the resort provides a ferry service to and from the mainland. Although the staff use four-wheel drive vehicles to access certain areas, cars are not allowed within the resort. For guests there are walking trails, bicycles and the ‘beach train’.

As an ecotourism-based resort, most of the planning and development has focused on the need to co-exist with the fragile natural environment of South Stradbroke Island. After the resort's construction, native vegetation was replanted to blend in with the environment aesthetically. In addition, all accommodation (eco-cabins) blends in with the existing landscape; this was achieved through the use of natural timbers and colour.

Given the warm and humid climate for nine months of the year, the cabins are built on stilts, allowing air to circulate under the buildings and thereby reducing the need for air conditioning. The verandahs have been fitted with screens to keep out mosquitoes. Visitors who stay at the resort are encouraged to monitor their water and energy usage by means of the television in their room, and are rewarded with prizes if their usage level is low.

Throughout the resort, walkways have been installed for conservation purposes. These do not restrict access to the natural environment but, as they are raised above the ground, they do keep people off the delicate forest floor. One part of the walkways includes a tower to allow visitors to view and appreciate the whole rainforest, from the canopy to the forest floor.

South Stradbroke Island has access to groundwater through a freshwater aquifer, or underground lake, which is recharged by rainfall. The resort obtains its water supply by tapping into this aquifer. Some of the problems which have threatened the island’s freshwater supply include contamination and overconsumption. In a bid to minimise this, all laundry activities are carried out on the mainland. The resort considers washing machines as onerous to the island’s freshwater supply, and the detergents contain a high level of phosphates which are a major source of water contamination.

The resort uses liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) to power its generators rather than a diesel-powered plant. The gas is supplemented by a wind turbine, which has reduced greenhouse emissions by 70% compared to diesel-equivalent generation methods. Hot water in the eco-cabins is solar-powered, as are some of the resort’s vehicles. Water-efficient fittings are also installed in showers and toilets.

Pest management is an important part of conservation. Couran Cove Resort has adopted a holistic approach to pests such as mosquitoes, which includes using natural predators as well as environmentally friendly solutions. This approach was widely practised initially, but the added pressure of increased visitors has resulted in the use of chemical treatments as a temporary measure.

Couran Cove Resort has implemented a range of environmental and cultural educational initiatives. The interpretive centre at the resort serves as a hub for information on all activities, including advice as to what visitors should and should not do. Development and human settlement have had negative impacts on some wildlife. For instance, there is evidence that wallabies have become accustomed to being fed by island visitors, which has caused the potentially fatal ‘lumpy jaws’ syndrome. Consequently, signage and verbal education are used throughout the resort to dissuade guests from feeding the native animals.

The resort has embraced and has effectively implemented contemporary environmental management practices. However, it does not conform to the model for development as proposed by Prideaux (2000). According to Prideaux, a resort should provide 3—4 star hotel-type accommodation for visitors mainly from interstate. While the accommodation is definitely at this level, the number of interstate and international tourists visiting the resort is small, with the principal markets comprising locals and residents from nearby towns. Marketing further afield should therefore be incorporated into the management strategy of the resort in order to meet this criterion.
